prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B029) first and the Higgs discovery (B039) second, but the opening ballots show that optical lattice clocks (B012) are the one candidate that nearly everyone rates highly and for compatible reasons: three first places, six top-three placements and all eight members ranking it. That is not merit in itself, so I tested the substance. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the dominant lattice light shift, and Ye's group pushed the resulting clocks to about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. The idea is original, the mechanism is clean, and the credit sits naturally with two people. Many independent laboratories and several species (Sr, Yb, Hg) reproduce the performance, and international clock comparisons are under way. The impact is concrete: tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter-like drifts, relativistic geodesy, and the prospective redefinition of the second. As an instrument builder I also value that this is a measurement capability that changes what can be done, not an interpretation that may be revised. I therefore move B012 from third to my preferred prize, ahead of B029.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the boundary with earlier recognition and parallel work. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control) already cover adjacent ground, and optical ion clocks are a parallel line that this entry does not credit. Several groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, JILA colleagues, and others in Japan) contributed to making lattice clocks work, so a two-name credit is a simplification. There is also a fair argument that a laureate-quality discovery in fundamental physics, such as IceCube or Higgs, carries more weight with the wider community than a precision-metrology achievement, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B012 first because lattice clocks combine magic-wavelength trapping with Lamb-Dicke confinement of many atoms, reach about 1e-18 and are confirmed across species and laboratories, so recognition is timely and the field stable.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and it is what moved me. I differ on his second choice: Kroll puts Cirac, Zoller and Blatt (B010) next, and I find that less compelling now. Wineland and Haroche were honoured in 2012 for control of single quantum systems, and the Cirac-Zoller gate has its decisive theoretical idea but a more diffuse experimental credit among several ion-trap groups. I would keep B010 off my list while accepting that it is mature.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and first strontium demonstration, together with Ye's high-accuracy implementations, are the two decisive contributions, and that the pending redefinition of the second makes recognition timely.
responses.response: I accept the two-person attribution. Her own caveat, that she relies on memory for early details and that ion clocks are a parallel line, is the right one. I would still hold that the citation should name the lattice clock specifically, so that it does not overreach into ion or microwave standards. I would not make the redefinition of the second a condition for the prize; the 1e-18 performance and its independent reproduction already stand on their own.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery (B039) first as a clear, concrete discovery that completes the electroweak sector, with a pragmatic three-name selection of Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti covering both detectors and the discovery period.
responses.response: I share his view that the Higgs discovery is among the most important experimental results and I ranked it second. But the attribution is the serious problem and I think his proposal underplays it. Choosing leaders of two collaborations of thousands is a judgment about roles rather than scientific authorship, and Della Negra's founding role in CMS is as strong as Virdee's. A prize that must exclude one of four credible founders, with both experiments represented by only partial leadership, is more contestable than a two-person clock prize. For this reason I keep B039 as an alternative and not my preferred prize this year.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B051) first, as the architecture behind superconducting quantum processors, but notes that the 2025 prize already recognised superconducting circuits, which bears on how much emphasis remains.
responses.response: I think his own caveat is decisive for me. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is close enough that giving circuit QED so soon would raise a legitimate question of overlap and balance, even though the physics is distinct and sound. I can see a case for B051 in a later year, but it is not a rival to B012 now. I also defer to his closer knowledge of the field on the Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff split, which I cannot check independently.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks giant tunnel magnetoresistance in MgO (B005) first, as a theory-plus-experiment success with large device impact, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B036) second with some worry about timing because the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with his worry on B036: reproduction is broad, but the interpretation is still moving, and that argues for patience. On B005 I accept the clear device impact and mature recognition. My reservation is credit, since Mathon and Umerski reached similar theoretical conclusions to Butler and the 2007 GMR prize sits close by. B012 has a cleaner attribution and a wider scientific reach beyond device engineering, which is why I place it ahead.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit lattice clocks as a stand-alone invention or fold in related precision-clock work, and how to handle the Hall, Hansch and Wineland boundary.

Whether contributions of other lattice-clock groups, and the roles of Katori versus Ye in the early realisations, are accurately summarised from colleagues' recollections; I have not verified them independently.
Whether the IceCube allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers can be made fairly enough to make B029 a serious competitor in a later round.
How much weight the committee should place on the redefinition of the second not yet having occurred.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B012. For disclosure, my work in cosmic-ray, gamma-ray and neutrino-adjacent astroparticle instrumentation and in large collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO, XL-Calibur) makes me close to the field of B029 and the collaboration-credit issue in B039, though the profile records no direct tie to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS or to any credited person.
